{{< include _score-kit.qmd >}}

Open an orchestral score and the viola line looks wrong: a strange bracket-shaped clef, and notes that
make no sense if you read them as treble or bass. That is the **alto clef**. A few staves lower, the
cello and bassoon may switch to the **tenor clef** for their high passages. Both are the same sign, the
**C clef**, placed on a different line. This lesson teaches you to read both.

## 1. One sign, movable: the C clef

Every clef is a letter that names one line. The treble clef is a G, and its curl wraps the line that is
G above middle C. The bass clef is an F, and its two dots sit either side of the line that is F below
middle C. The **C clef** points, with the middle of its bracket, at the line that is **middle C**.

The C clef can sit on any line. Two of those positions survive in everyday use:

| Clef | Middle C is on | Used by |
|---|---|---|
| **Alto** | the middle (3rd) line | viola; alto trombone; older music for alto voice |
| **Tenor** | the 4th line from the bottom | cello, bassoon and tenor trombone in their high range; sometimes double bass and euphonium |

Older music also has soprano clef (C on the bottom line), mezzo-soprano (2nd line) and baritone clef.
You meet them in early editions and in score-reading exams, rarely anywhere else.

Here is middle C in four clefs. Same sound, four different places on the staff:

<div class="abc-ex" data-sound="piano"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
L:1/1
K:C clef=treble
C | [K:clef=alto] C | [K:clef=tenor] C | [K:clef=bass] C |]
</script></div>

## 2. Why bother with another clef?

The answer is **ledger lines**. A viola's range runs from the C below middle C up through the middle
of the treble staff. In treble clef its lowest notes need three or four ledger lines below; in bass
clef its upper notes climb above the staff. The alto clef centres the staff on middle C, which is
roughly the middle of the viola, so almost everything it plays sits on the five lines.

The tenor clef does the same for the cello and bassoon's upper register: the passage that would hover
above the bass staff sits inside the tenor staff instead. Here is the same cello line in bass clef and
in tenor clef:

<div class="abc-ex" data-sound="piano"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:Bass clef
M:4/4
L:1/4
K:D clef=bass
A, B, C D | E F G A | F2 E2 | D4 |]
</script></div>

<div class="abc-ex" data-sound="piano"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:Tenor clef, same notes
M:4/4
L:1/4
K:D clef=tenor
A, B, C D | E F G A | F2 E2 | D4 |]
</script></div>

## 3. Reading alto clef

**The anchor.** The middle line is middle C. Learn the notes next to it: the space above is D, the
space below is B, the line above is E, the line below is A.

**The shortcut.** Read the note as if it were treble clef, then go **one letter up and an octave
down**. A note on the middle line would be B in treble clef; in alto clef it is C (the one below).

**Landmarks.** Bottom line F (below middle C), top line G (above middle C). Bottom space G, top space F.

Here is a familiar tune in alto clef, at viola pitch. Name the first four notes before you press ▶:

<div class="abc-ex" data-sound="piano"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
M:4/4
L:1/4
K:C clef=alto
E E F G | G F E D | C C D E | E3/2 D/2 D2 |]
</script></div>

<div class="sq" data-quiz="alto"></div>

## 4. Reading tenor clef

**The anchor.** The fourth line (one below the top) is middle C.

**Shortcut one.** Read it as bass clef, then go **up a fifth**. The middle line in bass clef is D; in
tenor clef it is A, a fifth higher.

**Shortcut two.** Read it as treble clef, then **one letter down and an octave lower**. The middle line
is B in treble; in tenor clef it is the A below middle C.

**Landmarks.** Bottom line D (an octave and a step below middle C), top line E (above middle C).

<div class="abc-ex" data-sound="piano"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
M:4/4
L:1/4
K:G clef=tenor
B, B, C D | D C B, A, | G, G, A, B, | B,3/2 A,/2 A,2 |]
</script></div>

<div class="sq" data-quiz="tenor"></div>

<div class="sr-tip">

**Do not read clefs by converting.** The shortcuts get you started. Real fluency comes from knowing
each clef's landmarks directly, the way you know treble clef. Ten minutes a day of the drills below,
for two weeks, does it.

</div>

## 5. All four clefs, mixed

Score reading means switching clef every staff. This drill shows treble, bass, alto or tenor at random.
